body_markdown:
Scurvy is often associated with centuries past, when sailors spent months at sea without access to fresh fruit and vegetables. In modern times, the condition is considered extremely uncommon, particularly in countries where fresh food and nutritional supplements are widely available.


That is why the death of a six-year-old boy in Queensland, Australia, has drawn attention to a condition many people may believe disappeared long ago.


The child, Connor Dean, died at Queensland Children's Hospital in Brisbane in August 2024. According to findings reported after his death, a severe vitamin C deficiency consistent with scurvy was associated with a heart attack that ultimately contributed to his death.


The case also raised important questions about childhood nutrition, selective eating and the difficulties doctors can face when a rare nutritional deficiency produces symptoms that resemble other serious illnesses.


## A condition rarely seen today


Scurvy develops when the body does not receive enough vitamin C over an extended period. Vitamin C plays an important role in maintaining healthy connective tissue, blood vessels and other parts of the body.


Historically, scurvy was a major health problem. Sailors on long voyages were particularly vulnerable because they could spend prolonged periods without fresh produce. The disease could cause serious physical problems and, in severe cases, become fatal.


Modern access to fruit, vegetables and vitamin supplements has made severe scurvy unusual. However, the condition has not completely disappeared.


Connor's case demonstrates that nutritional deficiencies can still occur, including in children whose families may believe they are receiving adequate nutritional support.


## Symptoms initially pointed doctors elsewhere


Connor had Down syndrome and a heart defect, alongside developmental difficulties. In July 2024, he was taken to a doctor after developing knee pain, a shuffling gait and limping. These symptoms were initially believed to be connected to a fall at the playground.


When his condition failed to improve, he was admitted to Queensland Children's Hospital. Doctors carried out X-rays and an MRI, but the investigations did not immediately reveal an obvious explanation for his worsening health.


He was diagnosed with para-influenza during this period. His mother also reported that he was taking a multivitamin and that his vaccinations were up to date.


As Connor's condition deteriorated, the situation became increasingly serious. On one occasion, he required resuscitation. Doctors considered the possibility of leukaemia, but that diagnosis was subsequently ruled out.


By the end of July, he was showing signs associated with renal disease, multiple organ failure and sepsis.


It was during this complicated progression that doctors began considering scurvy as a possible explanation for the combination of symptoms.


## Diet became an important part of the investigation


The case highlighted concerns that had existed around Connor's growth and diet for some time.


A doctor told the coroner that there had been longstanding concerns about his growth and height. Connor had previously been partially fed through a gastric tube and, according to the information presented to the coroner, his eating habits had become increasingly restrictive.


His mother said he had eaten a range of foods until around 2022. By 2023, however, a paediatrician described him as a very fussy eater.


The reported diet contained little or no fruit or vegetables. The paediatrician was concerned about both the amount of food Connor was consuming and whether he was receiving sufficient vitamins and minerals.


His weight gain was also limited. According to the evidence reported in the case, he gained only around 300 grams over an 11-month period.


These details underline an important point about nutrition. A child can consume food regularly while still failing to receive enough of particular nutrients.


## Why a multivitamin did not prevent the deficiency


One of the more complicated aspects of the case involved nutritional supplements.


Connor had been given supplements as part of efforts to address concerns about his nutrition. However, the particular multivitamin he was taking when admitted to hospital did not contain vitamin C.


Earlier medical advice had involved a specific multivitamin product. Another product used by Connor contained only a small amount of vitamin C, according to the evidence reported to the coroner.


Connor was also receiving other nutritional supplements and treatments, including vitamin D3, iron and vitamin A.


His parents told the coroner that they did not realise he had a specific vitamin C deficiency until it was too late.


The case therefore illustrates why the term "multivitamin" should not automatically be interpreted as meaning that every essential vitamin is present in meaningful amounts. The contents of supplements can vary, and product labels should be checked carefully.


## A difficult diagnosis


One reason this case was particularly challenging was the wide range of symptoms Connor experienced.


Knee pain, difficulty walking, weakness and serious systemic complications can potentially be associated with many different illnesses. Doctors initially investigated several possibilities, including infections and leukaemia.


The eventual recognition of severe vitamin C deficiency offered a possible explanation connecting symptoms that had previously appeared unrelated.


According to the coroner's findings, Connor died after invasive treatments were stopped. The reported cause involved a heart attack associated with severe vitamin C deficiency consistent with scurvy.


The case demonstrates how nutritional deficiencies can sometimes remain hidden behind more familiar or immediately concerning diagnoses.


## What parents and carers can learn


Connor's story should not be interpreted as a reason for parents to panic about ordinary picky eating. Many children go through periods of selective eating, and not every child who avoids certain foods will develop a serious deficiency.


However, persistent and extreme food restriction can become a nutritional concern, particularly when a child consistently avoids entire food groups.


Parents and carers may wish to discuss significant dietary restrictions with a GP, paediatrician or registered dietitian. Professional advice can help determine whether a child's diet is providing enough calories, vitamins and minerals.


Growth patterns can also provide useful information. If a child is not gaining weight or growing as expected, medical advice can help identify whether nutrition, an underlying condition or another factor may be involved.


For children with particularly restricted diets or additional medical needs, nutritional monitoring may be especially important.


## Why this case matters


The coroner reportedly said that publishing the findings could help draw attention to Connor's death and potentially prevent similar deaths in the future.


That is perhaps the most important lesson from this tragic case.


Scurvy may be associated with history books, long sea voyages and a time before modern food supplies. Yet severe vitamin C deficiency remains medically possible when nutritional needs are not adequately met.


Connor's death is a reminder that access to food is not necessarily the same as access to a balanced diet. It also shows why persistent concerns about growth, eating habits or unexplained symptoms deserve careful medical attention.


The case is not simply about a disease from the past returning. It is about recognising that nutritional health remains an important part of overall health, even in modern healthcare systems.


When a child has a highly restricted diet, unexplained physical symptoms or concerns about growth, early professional assessment can be valuable. In rare cases, identifying a nutritional deficiency may make the difference between a treatable condition and a devastating outcome.


## Source


Daily Mirror article concerning the death of six-year-old Connor Dean in Queensland, Australia, including evidence reported from the coroner's findings and statements from medical professionals involved in the case.
